records.name: Georgia
records.summary:
Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors — and deteriorating fast. In September 2024 parliament (the elected national assembly) passed the law “On the Protection of Family Values and Minors”: it bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, LGBT public assembly, and dissemination of LGBT information — the region’s harshest legislative package. One day after passage, Kesaria Abramidze, one of Georgia’s best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her apartment in the capital (Tbilisi); mourners and the news agency AP drew a direct line between the law’s rhetoric and the killing.

This compounds an existing pattern: the 2021 Pride office ransacking by far-right mobs while police stood by, the foreign-agents law choking local rights groups and LGBT NGOs (which refuse to register and face bankruptcy), and documented police failure to protect demonstrators (Identoba v. Georgia ECtHR line of cases before the regional human-rights court, still unimplemented). Georgia’s visible trans community is now legally erased and physically targeted.

For a visitor:

sources.summary: BBC (Sep 2024): trans model and influencer Kesaria Abramidze was killed just one day after the Georgian parliament passed the anti-LGBTI law; German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path.

AP (Oct 2024): 'Georgia's anti-LGBTQ+ measures raise fears of hate crimes in the conservative South Caucasus nation' — after the stabbing death of trans actress-model Kesaria Abramidze, Russia-style 'gay propaganda' laws stoke fear.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Georgia: the foreign agents law endangers LGBTI service provision (organisations refusing to register as 'foreign agents' face fines/bankruptcy); the anti-LGBTI law eroded trust, decreasing service applications; large numbers of LGBTI people are fleeing the country and seeking asylum documentation; misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

WISG et al. report to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers (5 Aug 2024) on implementation of LGBTI-rights decisions in Georgia: recommends urgent action — effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression.

IWPR Global Voices (May 2012): 'Georgian Laws Discriminate on Transgender Rights' - legal activists say the law should be changed to allow gender recognition; job applications become difficult when a person's gender identity doesn't match official paperwork - trans-specific legal barriers in Georgia.

OC Media (Jun 2019): Georgia's Interior Ministry declared Tbilisi Pride 'impossible' in the planned city-centre locations 'due to safety risks' (programme 18–23 June); organisers reported a week of pressure from an 'unidentified government official' to cancel the march, and far-right groups had vowed to thwart it — the country's first-ever pride.

records.name: Armenia
records.summary:
Armenia demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — Armenia has no anti-LGBT legislation of the restrictive type seen in neighbouring countries — and an administrative practice for legal gender recognition exists (medicalised). Pink Armenia’s 2024 annual report documents ongoing violations including inhuman/degrading treatment, and hate speech is routine in public discourse; the 2018 failed anti-discrimination bill means there is still no SOGI-specific (sexual orientation and gender identity) protection statute. The capital, Yerevan, has a small organised community (Pink Armenia and Right Side — a national rights organisation and a trans-led local group), but visibility carries real risk.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; social hostility significant outside central areas of the capital (Yerevan); police response unreliable; border and document-screening practice is not covered in the current sources.

sources.summary: Pink Human Rights Defender NGO annual report on the human rights situation of LGBT+ people in Armenia during 2024. Documents discrimination, torture and inhuman/degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion targeting LGBT people, violations of private and family life, education and work rights, and hate speech - including a chapter on pressure around a transgender individual participating in a beauty pageant.

Equaldex comparison of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia: Armenia decriminalised in 2003; legal gender change is legal but requires surgery (since 2006); gender-affirming care is restricted; no nonbinary recognition; hate-crime protections 'ambiguous' since 2022; no SOGI discrimination protections; same-sex marriage banned. Public-opinion acceptance scores are very low (5/100).

ILGA-Europe/COC fact-finding report 'Forced Out: LGBT People in Armenia' (Feb 2009): comprehensive mission report covering visibility, coming out, societal and institutional homophobia, media coverage, HIV/AIDS, discrimination, harassment and violence, community organising, and legislation affecting LGBT people in Armenia.

Unzipped: Gay Armenia blog (May 2012): neo-Nazi arson attack on the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan - Molotov cocktail thrown, fire set; police took 12 hours to respond; two suspects detained via CCTV - documents anti-LGBT hate violence in Armenia.

The Guardian (April 2019): Armenia's first registered trans woman, Lilit Martirosyan, received death threats (including MPs calling for her to be burned alive) after a historic speech in the national assembly on LGBTI discrimination - documents extreme political hostility toward trans people.

records.name: Azerbaijan
records.summary:
Azerbaijan is dangerous for trans visitors. The documented pattern is grim: a trans woman was tortured and murdered in the capital, Baku, in July 2023; a second trans woman’s murder in March 2024 was met with a police response lacking comprehensive investigation; several other trans people were physically assaulted, including by police themselves; and two trans women were detained for “hooliganism” for making noise. Government-affiliated media air targeted discriminatory hate speech.

Nothing formally criminalises gender expression, but police are perpetrators rather than protectors, and the state is one of the world’s more closed authoritarian systems — there is no recourse and no community infrastructure that can operate openly. An April 2024 ECtHR ruling (the regional rights-court) found violations in Azerbaijan’s treatment of LGBTI applicants.

For a visitor: no statute bars entry or expression, but discovery risks police abuse with no remedy, and the murder-impunity pattern is documented; border and document-screening practice is not detailed in the current sources.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Azerbaijan. Documents the March murder of a trans woman in Baku met with an inadequate police investigation; state-affiliated Real TV airing discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a Women's Day march demanding trans healthcare access; a family forcibly transporting an 18-year-old woman to Baku after she came out; and an April ECtHR ruling on the September 2017 police arrests and mistreatment of LGBTI people, which Azerbaijan acknowledged in 2019.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Azerbaijan. Documents a July police raid on a private birthday party where queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of outing; QueeRadar monitoring found 77% of 428 analysed media pieces hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people; and an activist being told to remove a rainbow flag in a Baku cafe.

OC Media feature by Ali Malikov on trans people in Azerbaijan: discrimination has direct economic impacts - trans people are rejected from jobs and housing, pushed into black-market work and precarious housing. Profiles 'Durdana', 29, arrested, denied housing and employment, and dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer shut down.

HRW (Oct 2017): Azerbaijan's anti-gay crackdown — police raids in Baku (Sept 2017) detained dozens of LGBT people on dubious charges with beatings documented; HRW called for investigation and release.

Gender & Development Social Union shadow report to CEDAW (44th session) on discrimination and violence against lesbian, bisexual and transgender people in Azerbaijan: documents state-approved ignorance, employment discrimination, militant homophobia/transphobia in official and private media, forced marriages, and the impossibility of changing identity documents for trans women; the organisation serves 200+ LBT people.

The Guardian (Sept 2017): outcry as Azerbaijan police launch crackdown on the LGBT community - at least 60 people imprisoned or fined after raids in the capital; part of a wave of arrests ahead of the Islamic Solidarity Games.

records.name: Kazakhstan
records.summary:
Kazakhstan demands real caution from trans visitors — Central Asia's most liveable country for trans people, a relative statement within its region. Nothing is criminalised: no propaganda statute, no bathroom law, and no police targeting pattern — police are unhelpful rather than predatory. Legal gender recognition exists but is heavily medicalised (psychiatric boards, surgery requirements applied in practice). An international monitoring body recorded 62 anti-LGBTI bias incidents in 2024 — real incidents, yet documented and reported, which itself signals a functioning civil society (Feminita, ECOM).

For a visitor: no legal exposure; low visibility keeps visitor exposure small; the main cities are navigable.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review covering Jan–Dec 2023 (Kazakhstan): documents access-to-services bias (an LGBTQI+ education NGO denied employment-site registration after listing its focus), bias-motivated violence (an LGBTQI activist almost run over with no investigation), and a wave of transgender people arriving from Russia since 2022.

OSCE/ODIHR Hate Crime Reporting 2024 summary for Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data to ODIHR since the 2018 report, has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes, and would benefit from victim-support and awareness measures — an institutional-gap finding on documentation of bias violence.

HRW (10 Jul 2024): in June 2024 the Ministry of Culture and Information said it was reviewing a 'We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!' petition (Union of Parents) that met the threshold for government consideration; HRW warns the proposed ban would violate rights nationwide — a live, dated legislative threat.

ECOM regional report library page (2024): ECOM has monitored and documented rights violations against LGBT people since 2017; the analysis identifies health-right barriers across the EECA region as a whole and in individual countries (incl. Kazakhstan), plus informal behavioural practices missed by policy analysis — abstract-level, country data is in the linked report body.

HRW (24 Sep 2019): Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation from a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments — privacy rights upheld over a 'moral foundations' defence; the women fled Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for safety, illustrating both the privacy remedy and the social risk.

records.name: Nicaragua
records.summary: Nicaragua is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans — sodomy was decriminalised in 2008 — but NGOs document 108 cases of violence against the LGBTIQ+ community in 2024 alone and 10 murders of trans women in the last two and a half years, and arbitrary detention is used broadly against perceived opponents. Since 2018 virtually all independent civil society has been shut down or exiled, so there is no domestic protection infrastructure and no recourse for a visitor facing harm.

sources.summary: thin: no usable finding

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report on Nicaragua: documents a police/parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived regime enemies that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among significant violations. For this record: official US assessment that anti-LGBTI abuse occurs inside a climate of state impunity.

Amnesty International (May 2019): the post-April-2018 protest crackdown left at least 325 dead and more than 2,000 injured per the IACHR; journalist Miguel Mora describes being beaten by a pro-government mob and being targeted partly for being gay, illustrating the intersection of political repression and homophobia. For this record: documented violence context and homophobia within the repression, with the casualty figures.

PinkNews (Nov 2007): Nicaragua's new penal code, effective March 2008, repealed the 1992 sodomy law (1-3 years' imprisonment), whose vague wording had also been usable against LGBT-rights campaigning and sexual-health work. For this record: dated decriminalisation — same-sex conduct not criminalised since 2008.

records.name: Suriname
records.summary:
Suriname is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors — legally unremarkable, socially mixed. Same-sex conduct is legal, the constitution's 'any other status' clause is read to cover SOGI discrimination, and the penal code has carried sexual-orientation discrimination and hate-speech provisions since March 2015. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-murder pattern, but the capital's small community reports routine harassment, and the interior has essentially no protection.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest street risk in the capital; low tourist infrastructure generally.

sources.summary: Country overview updated 12 Mar 2026: same-sex relations legal for men and women nationwide; legal gender recognition NOT possible; LGBTI organisations CAN register. Constitution Article 8.2's 'any other status' clause is read by the government as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity despite no explicit statutory protection.

Civil-society report of July 2024 (Projekta Foundation with VIDS and LGBT Platform): Constitution Article 8 covers SOGI only implicitly through 'any other status', and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since 1869. The LGBT Platform Suriname, founded 29 August 2011, unites PAREA, New Monday Foundation, Suriname Men United, Women's Way and Trans in Action; the report urges a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Suriname: documents the Bouterse trial, police brutality, corruption, and 'discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex (LGBTI) persons and other minorities'.

Submission to the UN Human Rights Committee (115th session) from LGBT Platform Suriname, Heartland Alliance and Akahata: despite constitutional protection LGBTI persons still face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatization. It records that in March 2015 Penal Code Articles 175, 175a and 176 were revised to cover discrimination and hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation.

Human Rights Committee review of Suriname, July 2024: the State asserted its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, backed by monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission, while experts pressed on implementing the Inter-American Court's judgment on transgender identity. The Committee welcomed abolition of the death penalty in the Penal Code (2015) and Military Code (2021).

UN UPR pre-session summary of March 2016 from the Suriname LGBT Platform: since the 2011 UPR the State revised the penal code to equalise the age of consent for same- and opposite-sex conduct and to add sexual-orientation discrimination provisions. The platform also reports it has been excluded from state consultative processes despite repeated requests.
